facts.numbers: every number in the voice, captions, card and file window passed both checkers; the bars measured exactly 23/40 and 2/40
concerns_a: 'My topic lost' plus the LOST stamp on a two-row card (mine vs the winner) can leave viewers thinking trades came last. It did not: automation-tools had 1 hot of 40 and small-business tied trades at 2. Literally true, so not a fail. Optional: 'My topic nearly came last.'

'keep the fastest AI videos from the last two weeks' can be heard as the fastest AI videos on all of YouTube. The tool kept the 40 fastest per area from what each area's searches returned. Optional: 'keep the fastest forty in each area from the last two weeks.'

Areas overlap: 16 areas x 40 kept = 640 but videos = 529, and area hot counts add to 195 against 148 total hot, so one video can count in more than one area (local-ai 23 and claude 21 may share videos). The ranking still holds as stated, but '23 of 40' is not 23 unique videos out of the 148.

Areas did not start from equal pools: local-ai searched 123 (fewest, 3 queries) vs agents-at-work 221. Each still kept 40, so 'of 40' is fair, but the winner was picked from the narrowest search pool.

The 12 'giant model on a laptop' videos come from the topic grouping across all 148 hot videos, not from the local-ai area. Placed right after 'AI you run on your own computer' wins, viewers may read the 12 as part of the 23. Not stated, so not a fail.

'Small channels can win' rests on a channel-relative test: hot means 3x that channel's own median, which a small channel with a low median clears more easily (the 20,000 floor limits this). Fine as an existence claim. It does not show small channels beat big ones.

'Hot' is not 'what people actually watch' in absolute terms: by views per day, market-news (21.0M views, 2.62M a day) dwarfs giant-model-on-laptop (3.5M, 421K a day). The video's 'winner' is by hot count, not by views. The card header says so, which is fine, but viewers may take 'winner' to mean most watched.

File window, 14.5-21.5 s: the note line is wrapped at a fixed width and clipped by the window edge, so it visibly reads 'Counts only: no / comment. The grouping of h... / a reading done in the Nov'. The words 'title, channel name or' are hidden, so on screen it looks like the note says 'no comment'. The text is real file text, not altered, but the clip changes how it reads.

Brand metrics slugs are dated 2026-11-14, -17 and -19, but their own reads are dated Nov 2 to Nov 12. The slug date is not a post date. The video shows none of these dates, so this does not affect the piece.

The brand's own videos got most of their views off YouTube (for example after-hours-robot: Instagram 1,295 vs YouTube 67). The count is YouTube only, which the video discloses ('YouTube only'), but it shows the count is not a test of the brand's own channels.
concerns_b: 'My topic lost' and the LOST stamp are true against the winner, but trades was not last: it tied small-business at 2, and automation-tools had 1. Any later wording that says 'last' or 'worst' would be false.

Only 3 trades searches were run (AI for contractors, AI for home service business, AI estimating construction), and 148 videos were searched against 205 for claude. 'Cold topic' rests on 3 queries in one 14-day pull. The caveat at 47.4 s covers pull and period, not query count.
The local-ai area includes the query 'open source AI model', which is not only about running AI on your own computer. The 'AI you run on your own computer' label slightly narrows what the 23 covers.

File window at 15.0 to 21.5 s: the note line is clipped at the right edge, so it reads '"note": "Counts only: no' then 'comment. The grouping of h...'. The hidden words 'title, channel name or' make it look like 'no comment.' Not a misquote, but a clipped view.

The highlight boxes (orange, teal, red) in the file window are drawn by the maker. They read clearly as annotation, and the text under them matches the source byte for byte as far as shown. The 'OUR FILE' window looks like a screen capture; its text matches the source files, so this is acceptable.

At 9.0 s the caption '62' appears over the queries.json window, which does not contain the number 62. The number comes from results.json 'searches' and also equals the query count in queries.json, so the value is correct.
The slugs of the three metrics records carry dates (11-14, 11-17, 11-19) later than their read dates (Nov 2 to Nov 12). This is probably a naming scheme, but it can't be explained from the files.

No em or en dashes seen on screen; hyphens appear only inside JSON keys, file names and dates. No private person or private channel is named; ChatGPT, OpenAI, Claude and YouTube appear only as search terms, area keys or platform names.
not_checked: Frames between the two-a-second samples were not seen; a brief on-screen element shown for under 0.5 s could be missed.

A dash check there is limited to what could be read. No em or en dash was seen anywhere: captions, card text and file-window text use only hyphens inside JSON keys and dates.

Whether every kept video is actually about AI, and how the 12 laptop videos were classified: titles are sealed and not in the files.

Whether the brand's posted videos are about 'AI for the trades': the three records hold view counts and slugs only (ai-night-quote, after-hours-robot, ask-chatgpt), with no subject field. They confirm three posted AI videos, not that the subject is the trades.

Whether the brand's videos are 'AI for the trades': the records have no subject or description field. They confirm only that three videos were posted and got views on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. The thumbnails show an AI receptionist, a late-night quote reply for a move-out clean, and a ChatGPT recommendation, which suggests home-service AI, but the files cannot confirm it.
